CAL POLY EMPOWER · SEPT 2025 – PRESENT

Assistive Arthritis Device

A spring-based, torque-balancing elbow tray designed with and for Christina, the parent of a Cal Poly student living with chronic osteoarthritis pain.

ROLEMechanical Designer
TOOLSSolidWorks, Fusion 360, FDM
SCOPEDesign + prototyping + client testing
TEAMEMPOWER Student Association
Elbow tray - ergonomic CAD design

The brief

Christina suffers from chronic pain due to osteoarthritis in her right elbow and hand. The goal was a device that provides an upward force on her forearm to support everyday movement, reducing the stress on her elbow by counterbalancing the weight of her own arm - something she could put on and use without help.

Preliminary design

Our first pass hung off the waist and shoulder with a telescoping mechanism and a single torsion spring. In testing it was too bulky, restricted some motion, and was uncomfortable to wear for any length of time - useful failure, but a failure we needed to design away from.

Redesign: arm-supported, two springs

I worked on the shift from a back-supported to a fully arm-supported design to cut out variables and get the device off Christina's shoulder entirely. The current design attaches only to the arm, is compact and portable, relieves the elbow directly, and allows a full range of motion with 60 degrees of wrist rotation - using two torsion springs instead of one.

The assembly breaks into three parts I designed and iterated together:

  • Bicep connection - attaches to the bicep and extrudes toward the elbow at an angle, housing the torsion spring at its end.
  • Forearm connection - houses the second torsion spring, connects to the bicep piece via a rod, and attaches to the forearm with a cup.
  • Torsion springs - connected between the bicep and forearm pieces at the elbow; their torque counterbalances the weight of the forearm.
Spring-based component integrated into the assembly to counteract the client's arm weight

Static equilibrium analysis

To size the torsion springs correctly, I ran static equilibrium analysis on the arm-tray system to validate moment balance across the full range of motion - the spring has to counteract the forearm's weight at every angle the elbow moves through, not just one static position.

Taking the sum of moments about the elbow pivot, the required spring torque turns out to depend on the sine of the rotation angle. A simple pulley with a constant radius can only apply constant torque for a given spring force, so it can't track that sine relationship on its own. The math showed the pulley radius itself needs to vary with the angle of rotation to match the torque the arm actually needs at each position, which is what led us to an irregularly shaped (non-circular) pulley instead of a standard round one.

Static equilibrium calculations, moment balance about the elbow pivot
3D-printed prototype - bicep and forearm supports, PETG

Prototyping & manufacturing

I built iterative assemblies in both SolidWorks and Fusion 360 and drove rapid prototyping cycles through FDM 3D printing, mostly in PETG. Small manufacturing details mattered here too - we cut the legs of our torsion springs down with a bolt cutter to fit the housing geometry. Looking ahead, we're considering switching to TPU for a more rubbery, ductile feel, and adding foam padding between the cups and Christina's skin for comfort.

Testing protocol

  • Confirm the torsion spring is seated properly in its housing.
  • Flex the device to stretch the torsion spring through its range.
  • Wrap the bicep strap first to anchor the device to the upper arm.
  • Wrap the forearm cup around the forearm.
  • Adjust the device as needed for fit.
  • Interview the user while she uses the product to capture qualitative feedback.

Presenting the work

I presented validation data and design rationale at both Preliminary Design Review (PDR) and Critical Design Review (CDR), demonstrating quantified performance improvements across design revisions to faculty reviewers.
